title: Love, the path
hookLine: love is the path the Tenth Guru said finds the Lord

lines: A HERON, STILL AS A MONK.
cards: A heron stands in shallow water at the edge of a pond. Perfectly still. One leg tucked up, eyes half closed, neck curved like a monk bowing in prayer.
From the bank it looks perfectly at peace. Then a fish swims near, and the stillness ends in a flash. It was never meditating.
It was waiting for lunch. Guru Gobind Singh, the Tenth Guru, used that bird in a verse. He asked what all our holy-looking stillness is worth, and gave one plain answer to everyone listening: prem.

teach.h: THE HERON: HOLY FROM THE BANK.
teach.b: First, the heron. In the Tav Prasad Swayye, which Sikhs recite among their morning prayers, the Tenth Guru asks, in paraphrase: what does it matter if you shut your eyes and sit like a heron in meditation?
He goes on through other outward feats: wandering from sea to sea to bathe, losing this world and the next along the way. Each can look holy from the bank. Each can be a heron.
Second, the answer, a line you met early on this path: jin prem keeo tin hee prabh paaeio.

teach.h: ONLY THOSE WHO LOVED FOUND THE LORD.
teach.b: In paraphrase: I tell you the truth, all of you, listen: only those who have loved have found the Lord. The word is prem: love. Not ritual first.
Not display first. Love. Third, love has a price.
Guru Nanak said it too, in a salok kept near the end of the Granth.
In paraphrase: if you long to play the game of love, come to my lane with your head on your palm; once you set foot on this path, give your head and don't hesitate. That's not soft romance.
It's love that costs everything and doesn't look back. Fourth, an ordinary day. Prem changes the question under a practice.
Not, did I pray long enough, or did I look devout, but, was there love in it?

teach.h: JIN PREM KEEO TIN HEE PRABH PAAEIO.
teach.b: A Sikh can recite every bani and still be a heron. Someone can stumble through one line with a full heart and be found. This isn't the Guru throwing out discipline; he wrote prayers Sikhs recite in the morning.
It's the Guru naming what the discipline is for.

how: The Tav Prasad Swayye is among the morning prayers Sikhs recite, and the line on love, jin prem keeo tin hee prabh paaeio, is sung in kirtan.

o: love, the path that finds the Lord beneath every ritual
a still, heron-like posture held in meditation
a lifelong vow of devotion to one teacher

games.q: what's inside prem: tap the pairs.

s: the Tenth Guru says long meditation alone finds the Lord
he says a person can sit like a heron; only those who have loved have found the Lord.
Guru Nanak said the game of love means coming with your head on your palm
in a salok near the end of the Granth: give your head and don't hesitate.
the line on love throws out discipline and prayer
the Tenth Guru wrote prayers people recite; the line names what discipline is for.

games.q: you're watching a heron, perfectly still in the water, eyes half closed. what is it doing?
games.why: the Guru's point: holy-looking stillness can be a heron's. only those who have loved have found the Lord.

practice: Bring to mind one person you love but rarely say it to: a parent, a sibling, an old friend, a child who's grown. Let their face stay with each in-breath, and on each out-breath send them whatever love is there.
If you pray, you can hold them before the Lord.

wordCard.voice: Prem. Love; in the Tenth Guru's swayya, the path that finds the Lord, beneath every ritual and every outward show. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: prem, love, the word in jin prem keeo tin hee prabh paaeio.

carryVoice: Your line: those who loved, found. Not the heron's stillness, but a full heart. That's today, done.

sources.ref: Tav Prasad Swayye (Akal Ustat, Guru Gobind Singh): kahaa bhaio jo dou lochan moond kai baith rahio bak dhiaan lagaaio ... saach kahoon sun leho sabhai jin prem keeo tin hee prabh paaeio
Ang 1412 (Salok Vaaraan te Vadheek, Guru Nanak: jau tau prem khelan kaa chaao, sir dhar talee galee meree aao)
